question:
Match the following:

(a) First gold coins  (i) Guptas

(b) Purest gold coins  (ii) Indo-Greeks

(c) Maximum number of gold coins  (iii) Kushanas
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-ii, b-iii, c-i: the Indo-Greeks issued the first gold coins, the Kushanas (Kanishka) the purest gold coins and the Guptas the maximum number of gold coins (पहले — इंडो-ग्रीक, शुद्धतम — कुषाण, सर्वाधिक — गुप्त)

 

• The Indo-Greek king Menander is associated with the introduction of gold coinage in India.

 

• Kushana gold coins of Kanishka were remarkable for their high purity and the variety of deities shown on them.

 

• The Guptas issued gold coins called Dinaras in large numbers, which is why their age is also described as rich in coinage.

 

• The sequence Indo-Greeks, Kushanas and Guptas follows the chronological order of the three dynasties.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kushana coins show Greek, Zoroastrian and Indian gods, including Shiva with Nandi on coins of Wima Kadphises.

 

• Gupta coins show kings as archers, lyre players and horse-sacrificers.

 

• Roman gold coins also reached India through trade in this period.

 

• Remember the order Indo-Greeks then Kushanas then Guptas for quantity and quality of gold coins.

 

• Kanishka's coins carry the figures of Buddha, Shiva and Zoroastrian deities.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii (Option 1): This pairing gives the first gold coins to the Guptas and the maximum number to the Kushanas, which reverses the chronology. The Guptas came centuries later and issued the most gold coins.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-ii (Option 3): This pairing is wrong because it gives the first gold coins to the Kushanas and the purest to the Guptas. The Indo-Greeks came first, and Kanishka's Kushana issues were the purest.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii (Option 4): This pairing is wrong because it keeps the Indo-Greeks as the first issuers but gives the purest coins to the Guptas and the maximum to the Kushanas. The correct pairs are Kushanas for purity and Guptas for quantity.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Sakas (Scythians):

1. They attacked Bactria and Parthia and took them from the Greek rulers.

2. They took the place of the Indo-Greeks in India.

3. They were a branch of the Yuchi tribe.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 stand correct: the Sakas attacked Bactria and Parthia, wrested them from the Greek rulers and so took the place of the Indo-Greeks in India; the branch of the Yuchi tribe is the Kushanas, so statement 3 is false (शक — इंडो-ग्रीक के उत्तराधिकारी)

 

• The Sakas are also called Scythians and came from Central Asia into north-western and western India.

 

• The Kushanas, not the Sakas, were a branch of the Yuchi tribe, who later replaced the Sakas in the north-west.

 

• A line of Saka rulers known as the Western Kshatrapas ruled Gujarat, Malwa and Saurashtra, with Rudradaman as their greatest king.

 

• The Saka rulers adopted Indian names and the Sanskrit language over time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Western Kshatrapas continued to rule till about the 4th century AD, when Chandragupta II defeated them.

 

• Saka rule in Ujjain is linked to the later Vikrama and Saka era traditions.

 

• Kanishka's Saka Era of 78 AD is also called by this name, though he was a Kushana.

 

• The Saka kings at Ujjain were Western Kshatrapas who ruled Saurashtra, Malwa and Gujarat.

 

• The Sakas were also called Scythians, who came from the steppes of Central Asia.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This pairing includes statement 3 along with statement 2, but statement 3 is wrong because the Kushanas, not the Sakas, were a branch of the Yuchi. It also leaves out statement 1.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This selection takes statements 1 and 3 but drops statement 2. Statement 2 is correct, as the Sakas replaced the Indo-Greeks, and statement 3 is wrong since the Yuchi branch was the Kushanas.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Here the option accepts all three statements, but statement 3 is false. The Sakas and the Yuchi-branch Kushanas were distinct peoples with different histories in India.

question: Rudradaman, the most famous Saka ruler of western India, bore which title?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mahakshatrapa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rudradaman, the greatest of the Western Kshatrapa Sakas, bore the title Mahakshatrapa (great satrap), which showed his high rank among the Saka rulers (रुद्रदामन — महाक्षत्रप की उपाधि)

 

• He ruled over Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa and is remembered for his strong rule and his Sanskrit inscription.

 

• He fought the Satavahanas and defeated them, according to his Junagadh inscription.

 

• His Junagadh (Girnar) inscription is the first long inscription in pure Sanskrit and records the repair of the Sudarshana Lake.

 

• Saka rulers used the titles Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa, the satrap titles taken from Iranian practice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Devaputra was the title adopted by Kushana kings such as Wima Kadphises and Kanishka.

 

• Dakshinapatheshvara was the title of Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas.

 

• Saka coins and inscriptions help in dating the Kshatrapa rulers.

 

• Saka rulers used the satrap titles Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa, adopted from Iranian practice.

 

• Rudradaman was a contemporary of the Satavahana ruler Vashishthiputra Pulamayi.

 

NOTE

 

• Devaputra (Option 2): Devaputra, meaning son of God, was the title adopted by Kushana rulers to claim divine status. It was not the title of the Saka ruler Rudradaman.

 

• Dakshinapatheshvara (Option 3): Dakshinapatheshvara, meaning Lord of the South, is associated with Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty in a later age. Rudradaman, a Saka, did not use it.

 

• Chakravartin (Option 4): Chakravartin means universal emperor and is a general imperial ideal in Indian tradition. It was not the characteristic title of Rudradaman, who is known as Mahakshatrapa.

question: The Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of Rudradaman is historically important because it is:
option_1: The earliest inscription in the Tamil language
option_2: The first long inscription written in pure Sanskrit
option_3: An edict of Ashoka on dhamma written in Prakrit
option_4: A Gupta prashasti written on an iron pillar
solution_text:
The correct answer is The first long inscription written in pure Sanskrit.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of Rudradaman in Gujarat is the first and longest inscription in pure Sanskrit of its time (जूनागढ़ अभिलेख — शुद्ध संस्कृत का पहला लंबा अभिलेख)

 

• Earlier inscriptions, like the Ashokan edicts, were mostly in Prakrit, so the shift to Sanskrit marks a new stage of literary language.

 

• The inscription gives details of the achievements of Rudradaman and mentions the repair of the Sudarshana Lake.

 

• It is found near Junagadh in Gujarat and is also called the Girnar rock inscription.

 

• It shows how the foreign Saka rulers adopted Indian culture and language.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same rock at Junagadh also bears an Ashokan edict.

 

• Sanskrit inscriptions became common in the Gupta period, as seen in the Allahabad Pillar prashasti.

 

• The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela is in Prakrit.

 

• The inscription is dated in the Saka era year 72, which corresponds to 150 AD.

 

• It mentions the repair of the Sudarshana Lake after a heavy flood broke its embankment.

 

NOTE

 

• The earliest inscription in the Tamil language (Option 1): The earliest Tamil inscriptions are in Tamil-Brahmi and belong to the south, not to the Junagadh rock in Gujarat. The Junagadh inscription is a Saka record, in Sanskrit.

 

• An edict of Ashoka on dhamma written in Prakrit (Option 3): Ashokan edicts on dhamma were written in Prakrit, and the Junagadh rock does carry one, but the Rudradaman inscription is a separate later record. It is written in Sanskrit, not Prakrit.

 

• A Gupta prashasti written on an iron pillar (Option 4): A Gupta prashasti on an iron pillar would refer to the Delhi Iron Pillar or the Allahabad pillar of the Gupta age. The Junagadh inscription is a Saka record on a rock, from earlier times.

question: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman records the repair of which lake in Gujarat?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sudarshana Lake.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman records that he repaired the Sudarshana Lake, a reservoir in the Girnar region of Gujarat that had been breached by a flood (सुदर्शन झील — रुद्रदामन द्वारा मरम्मत)

 

• The lake was an old irrigation work of the Mauryan age, which shows the continuity of Indian water management under foreign rulers.

 

• The inscription is written in pure Sanskrit and is the first and longest such inscription.

 

• It is also called the Girnar rock inscription because it is located near Mount Girnar close to Junagadh.

 

• Rudradaman held the title Mahakshatrapa and ruled the Western Kshatrapa kingdom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same rock carries Ashokan edicts, Rudradaman's inscription and a later Gupta record of Skandagupta.

 

• The Sudarshana Lake was repaired again by Skandagupta's governor Parnadatta.

 

• Irrigation works of this kind helped agriculture and revenue in the Saurashtra region.

 

• The Sudarshana Lake was first built in Mauryan times under the governor Pushyagupta, during Chandragupta Maurya's rule.

 

• Ashoka's governor Tushaspa added canals to the lake, as the same Junagadh inscription records.

 

NOTE

 

• Dal Lake (Option 1): Dal Lake lies in Kashmir and has no connection with the Junagadh inscription of Gujarat. The lake repaired by Rudradaman was in the Girnar region, far from Srinagar.

 

• Pushkar Lake (Option 2): Pushkar Lake in Rajasthan is a sacred lake and a pilgrimage site, but it is not mentioned in the Junagadh inscription. The record deals with a Gujarat reservoir.

 

• Chilika Lake (Option 4): Chilika Lake is a large lagoon on the coast of Odisha, in the east. The Junagadh inscription concerns Gujarat in western India, so it cannot refer to Chilika.

question: The Kushanas, who rose to power in north-western India, were originally a branch of which Central Asian tribe?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yuchi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kushanas were one branch of the Yuchi (Yueh-chi) tribe, whose original home was Central Asia, before they moved south and set up a large empire in north-western India (कुषाण — यूची जनजाति की शाखा)

 

• The Yuchi were pushed westward by other nomadic groups, and the Kushana branch finally settled in Bactria before entering India.

 

• The dynasty was founded by Kujula Kadphises, also called Kadphises I, and reached its peak under Kanishka.

 

• The Kushana empire extended over parts of Central Asia, Afghanistan, the north-west and the Gangetic plain, with capitals at Purushapura and Mathura.

 

• Their period saw great growth in trade on the Silk Route, in Buddhist art and in gold coinage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kushana rulers followed the Sakas and Parthians in north-western India.

 

• Kanishka's empire was among the largest of its time, linking India with Central Asia and Rome through trade.

 

• The Kushana period saw Mahayana Buddhism develop under royal patronage.

 

• Kushana rule over north-western India followed that of the Sakas and Parthians in the first century AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Sakas (Option 1): The Sakas were a separate Scythian people who preceded the Kushanas in India and ruled in western India as Kshatrapas. They were not the tribe from which the Kushanas came.

 

• Parthians (Option 3): The Parthians were a distinct Iranian people who held parts of north-western India for a time, and are known as Pahlavas. They are not the tribe of the Kushana origin.

 

• Huns (Option 4): The Huns came much later, in the 5th and 6th centuries AD, and were responsible for the fall of the Gupta empire. They have no role in the Kushana origin.

question: Who was the founder of the Kushana dynasty in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kujula Kadphises.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kujula Kadphises, also called Kadphises I, was the founder of the Kushana dynasty, who united the Yuchi tribes and began Kushana rule in the north-west (कुजुल कडफिसेस — कुषाण वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• His son Wima Kadphises extended the empire in India and issued gold coins showing Shiva and Nandi.

 

• The most famous Kushana ruler was Kanishka, who made Purushapura (Peshawar) his capital and started the Saka Era in 78 AD.

 

• The Kushanas adopted the title Devaputra, meaning son of God, to give their rule divine standing.

 

• The dynasty was one of the most important foreign dynasties to rule in India after the Mauryas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kujula Kadphises issued copper coins imitating Roman and Indo-Greek types.

 

• Huvishka succeeded Kanishka and ruled for many years, issuing gold coins with many deities.

 

• The last great Kushana ruler was Vasudeva I, whose name is Indian, showing cultural assimilation.

 

• The Kushana dynasty ruled for about two centuries, from the first to the third century AD, over a large area.

 

NOTE

 

• Kanishka (Option 2): Kanishka was the greatest Kushana king, but he came later in the dynasty and did not found it. He built on the empire that earlier Kushana kings had created.

 

• Wima Kadphises (Option 3): Wima Kadphises was the son of Kujula Kadphises and the second ruler, who expanded the dynasty. He inherited a state that had already been founded by his father.

 

• Huvishka (Option 4): Huvishka was a successor of Kanishka who ruled after him, so he lived a long time after the dynasty began. He was not its founder.

question: What title did many Kushana rulers adopt to signify their divine status?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Devaputra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Many Kushana rulers adopted the title Devaputra, meaning Son of God, to claim divine status and legitimise their rule (देवपुत्र — कुषाण शासकों की उपाधि)

 

• The title shows the influence of Central Asian and Chinese ideas of kingship, where rulers were seen as sons of heaven.

 

• Wima Kadphises and Kanishka are among the Kushana kings who used this title.

 

• Kushana kings also placed images of deities on their coins, which added to the divine aura of royalty.

 

• The use of grand titles by Kushana kings shows the stronger claims of kingship in the post-Mauryan period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kushana rulers also used the Iranian title Shahanushahi (king of kings) in some inscriptions.

 

• Kushana royal temples and statues, such as the statue of Kanishka at Mat near Mathura, show royal cult practices.

 

• Later Indian kings adopted titles like Maharajadhiraja, used by the Guptas.

 

• Kushana coin legends used Greek script at first and later the Bactrian language.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajadhiraja (Option 1): Rajadhiraja means king of kings and was used by several rulers, but it does not by itself convey divine status. The Kushana title that claimed divine descent was different.

 

• Chakravartin (Option 3): Chakravartin means universal ruler and is a general ideal of Indian kingship, not the specific Kushana title that proclaimed that the ruler was a son of God.

 

• Maharajadhiraja (Option 4): Maharajadhiraja, meaning great king of kings, was a title popular with the Gupta rulers. It denoted supreme political power, not divine descent as Devaputra did.

question:
Consider the following statements about Wima Kadphises:

1. He was the son of Kujula Kadphises.

2. He was a devotee of Lord Shiva.

3. He issued coins showing Shiva and the bull Nandi.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Wima Kadphises was the son of Kujula Kadphises, a devotee of Lord Shiva, and issued coins showing Shiva with Nandi (विम कडफिसेस — शिव भक्त, शिव और नंदी के सिक्के)

 

• He adopted the title Devaputra, showing the Kushana claim to divine status.

 

• His gold coins mark an early stage of Kushana gold coinage, which later reached its purest form under Kanishka.

 

• The Shiva and Nandi figures on his coins show that the Kushanas accepted Indian religious symbols.

 

• He expanded Kushana power into north-western India after his father, Kujula Kadphises, founded the dynasty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shiva appears on Kushana coins with the bull Nandi, the trident and sometimes the ithyphallic form.

 

• Kanishka's coins show Buddha, Shiva and Iranian gods.

 

• The Kushana kings thus supported many religions at the same time.

 

• The Kushana period saw the use of copper and gold coins in large numbers across north India.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): The chosen option takes only statements 1 and 2 as correct and rejects statement 3. Statement 3 is also true, as his coins display Shiva and Nandi, so this choice is incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): This alternative takes only statements 2 and 3 as correct and rejects statement 1. Statement 1 is also true, since Wima was the son of the dynasty's founder, Kujula Kadphises.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): This response takes only statements 1 and 3 as correct and rejects statement 2. Statement 2 is also true, as he was a devotee of Shiva, which is why he used the god on coins.

question:
Consider the following statements about Kanishka:

1. His capital was Purushapura, modern Peshawar.

2. Mathura was his second capital.

3. He was the founder of the Kushana dynasty.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Correct statements are 1 and 2: Kanishka had his capital at Purushapura (Peshawar) and his second capital at Mathura; statement 3 is wrong as the dynasty was founded by Kujula Kadphises (कनिष्क — पुरुषपुर और मथुरा)

 

• Kanishka is called the Second Ashoka for his great patronage of Buddhism.

 

• He started the Saka Era in 78 AD, and also convened the Fourth Buddhist Council.

 

• His coins are known as the purest Kushana gold coins.

 

• Gandhara and Mathura schools of art flourished under his patronage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Purushapura was an important city of Gandhara on the trade routes to Central Asia.

 

• Kanishka's stupa at Purushapura was a very tall structure described by Chinese travellers.

 

• Kanishka's empire stretched from Central Asia to the Gangetic plain.

 

• The Saka Era is used in official calendars and for dating many inscriptions of the early medieval Deccan.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This grouping includes statement 3, which is false since Kujula Kadphises founded the dynasty, and it drops statement 1, which is correct about the capital Purushapura.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This choice accepts statements 1 and 3 but rejects statement 2. Statement 2 is correct because Mathura was Kanishka's second capital, and statement 3 is false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This answer accepts all three, but statement 3 is wrong. Kanishka did not found the Kushana dynasty; Kujula Kadphises did, and Kanishka later became its greatest king.

question: The Saka Era (AD 78), used as the basis of India's national calendar, was started by which king?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kanishka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Saka Era beginning in AD 78 is traditionally associated with the Kushana king Kanishka, and is the basis of India's National Calendar (शक संवत 78 ई. — कनिष्क द्वारा प्रारंभ)

 

• Kanishka ruled from Purushapura (Peshawar), with Mathura as his second capital.

 

• He is called the Second Ashoka because of his patronage of Buddhism and the Fourth Buddhist Council.

 

• Kanishka's reign saw the flourishing of Gandhara and Mathura art.

 

• The Saka Era should not be confused with the Vikrama Samvat, which begins in 57 BC.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vikrama Samvat dates from 57 BC and the Gupta Era from AD 319-320.

 

• The Saka Era is used by the Government of India in its official calendar.

 

• Kanishka's rule is generally placed from AD 78 to about AD 100-120 in many books.

 

• Adoption of the national calendar in 1957 followed the report of the Calendar Reform Committee led by Meghnad Saha.

 

NOTE

 

• Ashoka (Option 1): Ashoka was a Mauryan emperor who lived in the third century BC, long before AD 78. He did not start any era of the kind and is known for his edicts and dhamma.

 

• Samudragupta (Option 2): Samudragupta was a Gupta king of the fourth century AD, long after 78 AD. The Gupta Era is associated with his dynasty, but not the Saka Era.

 

• Harsha (Option 4): Harsha ruled in the seventh century AD, centuries after the Saka Era began. He is known for his Pushyabhuti dynasty at Kannauj and the Harsha Era of 606 AD.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Indian National Calendar:

1. It is based on the Saka Era.

2. It was adopted on 22 March 1957.

3. The Saka Era began in 78 BC.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The true statements here are 1 and 2: the Indian National Calendar is based on the Saka Era and was adopted on 22 March 1957; statement 3 is false because the Saka Era began in 78 AD, not 78 BC (राष्ट्रीय कैलेंडर — शक संवत, 22 मार्च 1957)

 

• The Saka Era is traditionally linked with the Kushana king Kanishka.

 

• The national calendar starts the year with the month of Chaitra, which usually begins on 22 March (21 March in a leap year).

 

• The date of adoption, 22 March 1957, fell in the first decade after independence.

 

• The mix-up between 78 AD and 78 BC is a common trap in exam options.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Saka Era year is 78 years behind the Gregorian year in most months.

 

• The Vikrama Samvat begins in 57 BC and is widely used in north India.

 

• The Gupta Era began in AD 319-320.

 

• Kanishka's Fourth council reportedly compiled commentaries on the Buddhist scriptures, and the Mahavibhasa is linked to it.

 

• Kashmir was a major centre of Buddhist learning in the Kushana age.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This pairing takes statements 2 and 3 as correct, but statement 3 is false because the era began in AD 78. It also leaves out statement 1, which is true.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This selection takes statements 1 and 3 as correct, but statement 3 is false and statement 2 is true, so the combination is wrong.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Here the option takes all three statements as correct, but statement 3 is wrong since the Saka Era started in 78 AD and not in 78 BC.

question: The Fourth Buddhist Council, convened by Kanishka, was held at which place?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kundalavana, near Srinagar in Kashmir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Fourth Buddhist Council was held at Kundalavana monastery near Srinagar in Kashmir under the patronage of Kanishka, around 72 AD, with Vasumitra presiding (चतुर्थ बौद्ध संगीति — कुंडलवन, कश्मीर)

 

• It was called to settle questions of Buddhist theology and doctrine.

 

• After this council Buddhism split into two sects, Mahayana and Hinayana.

 

• Ashvaghosha is associated with this council as Vasumitra's deputy in later tradition.

 

• The council shows Kanishka's role as a patron of Buddhism, which earned him the title of the Second Ashoka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The first council was at Rajagriha, the second at Vaishali and the third at Pataliputra.

 

• The third council under Ashoka was presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa.

 

• Mahayana Buddhism introduced idol worship of the Buddha.

 

• The Mahayana ideal of the Bodhisattva, a being who delays his own nirvana to help others, grew in this period.

 

• Hinayana is now often called Theravada by Buddhists themselves.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajagriha (Option 1): Rajagriha was the site of the First Buddhist Council after the death of the Buddha. It belongs to the earliest phase of Buddhism, not to Kanishka's reign.

 

• Vaishali (Option 3): Vaishali hosted the Second Buddhist Council, about a century after the Buddha's death. It was held long before Kanishka's age, so it cannot be the place for the Fourth.

 

• Pataliputra (Option 4): Pataliputra was the venue of the Third Buddhist Council held under Ashoka in the third century BC. The Fourth council under Kanishka was held in Kashmir.

question: After the Fourth Buddhist Council, Buddhism split into two sects. Which feature is associated with the Mahayana sect?
option_1: Worship of the Buddha in idol form
option_2: Strict rejection of all images and rituals
option_3: Rule by the orthodox elders only
option_4: Complete reliance on the original teachings alone
solution_text:
The correct answer is Worship of the Buddha in idol form.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahayana, described as the 'new way of thinking', introduced the worship of Buddha idols, while Hinayana stands for the orthodox 'older tradition' without idol worship (महायान — बुद्ध मूर्ति पूजा)

 

• The split of Buddhism into Mahayana and Hinayana is linked to the period after the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka.

 

• The growth of Buddha images at Gandhara and Mathura is closely tied to the Mahayana development.

 

• Hinayana relied on the Buddha's original teachings and avoided idol worship.

 

• Mahayana spread widely to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan along the trade routes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Theravada Buddhism, linked with the Pali canon, is the surviving form of the older tradition.

 

• Mahayana texts were written in Sanskrit, such as Ashvaghosha's Buddhacharita.

 

• Nagarjuna's Madhyamika philosophy belongs to Mahayana.

 

• The Kushana period is the time when the Silk Route trade linked India, Central Asia, China and the Roman world.

 

NOTE

 

• Strict rejection of all images and rituals (Option 2): Strict rejection of images and rituals fits the older Hinayana tradition, which did not use idol worship, not the Mahayana, which introduced Buddha images and devotional worship.

 

• Rule by the orthodox elders only (Option 3): Reliance on rule by elders only describes the conservative school of Buddhism that is linked with Hinayana. Mahayana was a more open, devotional movement and is not characterised in this way.

 

• Complete reliance on the original teachings alone (Option 4): Complete reliance on the Buddha's original teachings alone is how the notes describe Hinayana. Mahayana added new ideas and the worship of the Buddha as a divine figure.

question: Which among the following statements is NOT true about Kanishka?
option_1: He patronized Buddhist scholars such as Vasumitra, Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna
option_2: He convened the Fourth Buddhist Council
option_3: Kanishka was succeeded by his son Vasudeva
option_4: The famous physician Charaka was patronized by him
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kanishka was succeeded by his son Vasudeva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The statement that Kanishka was succeeded by his son Vasudeva is not true; he was succeeded by Huvishka, and Vasudeva I ruled later in the Kushana line (कनिष्क का उत्तराधिकारी हुविष्क, वासुदेव नहीं)

 

• Kanishka patronised the Buddhist scholars Vasumitra, Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna, so the first statement is true.

 

• He convened the Fourth Buddhist Council at Kundalavana in Kashmir, around 72 AD.

 

• The physician Charaka, author of the Charaka Samhita, was patronised at his court.

 

• Vasudeva I, with an Indian name, shows the later Indianisation of the Kushana house.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Huvishka issued gold coins with a variety of deities.

 

• Vasudeva I was the last great Kushana ruler.

 

• Kanishka is called the Second Ashoka.

 

• Kanishka's capital Purushapura later became famous for a great stupa built under his patronage.

 

• Huvishka's long reign is known from inscriptions at Mathura and in Afghanistan.

 

• The Kushana line weakened after Vasudeva I and was later replaced by the Guptas and Sasanians in different regions.

 

NOTE

 

• He patronized Buddhist scholars such as Vasumitra, Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna (Option 1): That Kanishka patronised Vasumitra, Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna is true. Since the question asks for the statement that is NOT true, this accurate statement cannot be the answer.

 

• He convened the Fourth Buddhist Council (Option 2): That he convened the Fourth Buddhist Council is true; it was held in Kashmir under his patronage. A true statement cannot be the answer to a NOT-type question.

 

• The famous physician Charaka was patronized by him (Option 4): That Charaka the physician was patronised by Kanishka is true according to tradition. As it is a correct statement, it is not the answer to this NOT-type question.

question:
Match the following works with their authors:

(a) Buddhacharita  (i) Patanjali

(b) Charaka Samhita  (ii) Vasumitra

(c) Mahabhasya  (iii) Charaka

(d) Mahavibhasa  (iv) Ashvaghosha
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii: Buddhacharita by Ashvaghosha, Charaka Samhita by Charaka, Mahabhasya by Patanjali and Mahavibhasa by Vasumitra (बुद्धचरित — अश्वघोष, चरक संहिता — चरक, महाभाष्य — पतंजलि, महाविभाषा — वसुमित्र)

 

• Ashvaghosha was a great philosopher, poet and dramatist at the Kushana court, and his Buddhacharita is a poetic life of the Buddha.

 

• Charaka was a famous physician at Kanishka's court, and his Charaka Samhita is a treatise on medicine.

 

• Patanjali, the priest of Pushyamitra Sunga, wrote the Mahabhasya, a commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi.

 

• Vasumitra, a Buddhist scholar, wrote the Mahavibhasa and presided over the Fourth Buddhist Council.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Buddhacharita is written in Sanskrit and tells the life of the Buddha in epic style.

 

• The Charaka Samhita is a foundational text of Ayurveda, dealing mainly with internal medicine.

 

• Ashvaghosha also wrote the play Sariputraprakarana and the poem Saundarananda.

 

• Vasumitra, the author of the Mahavibhasa, was a Buddhist scholar of the Sarvastivada school in the Kushana age.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 1): This pairing gives the Charaka Samhita to Ashvaghosha and the Buddhacharita to Charaka, which swaps them. Charaka wrote about medicine, while Ashvaghosha was the poet who wrote the life of the Buddha.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii (Option 2): This pairing gives the Charaka Samhita to Patanjali and the Mahabhasya to Charaka, which is wrong. Patanjali was the grammarian of the Sunga age and Charaka the Kushana-age physician.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (Option 3): This pairing is wrong because it gives the Buddhacharita to Vasumitra and the Mahavibhasa to Ashvaghosha. Ashvaghosha wrote the Buddhacharita and Vasumitra the Mahavibhasa.

question:
Consider the following statements about Nagarjuna:

1. He is called the 'Einstein of India'.

2. He gave the philosophy of Sunyavada.

3. He wrote the Madhyamika Sutra.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Nagarjuna is called the Einstein of India, propounded Sunyavada and wrote the Madhyamika Sutra (नागार्जुन — शून्यवाद, माध्यमिक सूत्र)

 

• Nagarjuna was a great Mahayana Buddhist philosopher at the Kushana court of Kanishka according to the notes.

 

• Sunyavada (the doctrine of emptiness) is the central idea of the Madhyamika school of Mahayana Buddhism.

 

• His philosophy is also called the middle path, because it avoids extreme views about existence.

 

• He is one of the best known scholars of the Kushana age along with Ashvaghosha, Charaka and Vasumitra.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Madhyamika philosophy was later developed by thinkers like Chandrakirti.

 

• Sunya means void or emptiness in Sanskrit.

 

• Nagarjunakonda in Andhra is named after Nagarjuna in local tradition.

 

• Nagarjuna's best known work is the Mulamadhyamakakarika, which sets out the Madhyamika doctrine of emptiness.

 

• His teaching influenced Mahayana thought across Tibet, China and Japan.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): The chosen option accepts statements 1 and 2 but rejects statement 3. Statement 3 is also true, since the Madhyamika Sutra is credited to Nagarjuna in the notes.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): This alternative accepts statements 2 and 3 but rejects statement 1. Statement 1 is also true, because Nagarjuna is called the Einstein of India for his intellectual brilliance.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): This response accepts statements 1 and 3 but rejects statement 2. Statement 2 is true as well, since Sunyavada is the philosophy he propounded.

question: The Mathura school of art, famous for early Buddha images and red sandstone sculptures, flourished under which dynasty between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kushan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mathura school of art in modern Uttar Pradesh flourished under the Kushanas from the first century AD, producing early Buddha images in red sandstone (मथुरा कला — कुषाण काल)

 

• Its Buddha figures show a spiritual feeling in the face, which the Gandhara school largely lacked.

 

• The school produced images for both Indian and non-Indian patrons, and also for Jain and Hindu religions.

 

• The Gandhara school in the north-west, by contrast, mixed Indian and Greco-Roman elements.

 

• Both schools got royal patronage from Kanishka and the Kushana kings.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mathura was the Kushanas' second capital.

 

• The Mathura school continued to develop in the Gupta period with finer, more graceful figures.

 

• The Mat statue of Kanishka, found near Mathura, is a well-known work of this school.

 

• Mathura also yielded images of Jain Tirthankaras and Hindu deities during the Kushana age.

 

NOTE

 

• Mauryan (Option 1): The Mauryan period is known for polished stone pillars, lion capitals and Yaksha and Yakshi figures. It came earlier than the Mathura school, which began in the first century AD.

 

• Gupta (Option 2): The Gupta period is famed for a refined later phase of sculpture, but the early Buddha images of Mathura belong to the earlier Kushana age. The question's dates point to the Kushanas.

 

• Chola (Option 4): The Cholas ruled in South India in the medieval period and are known for bronzes and temples. They have no connection with the Mathura school of the first to third centuries.

question: The Gandhara school of art is best described as a blend of Indian elements with which of the following?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Greco-Roman elements.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gandhara school of art mixes Indian elements with Greco-Roman ones, and it is also known as the Indo-Greek school (गांधार कला — भारतीय और ग्रीको-रोमन तत्वों का मिश्रण)

 

• It began under the Indo-Greek rulers, but its real patrons were the Sakas and Kushanas, above all Kanishka.

 

• Its home is the region of Peshawar in north-western India, with sculptures found at Taxila, Peshawar and other places.

 

• The reliefs show scenes of the Buddha's birth, renunciation and preaching.

 

• The central theme is Mahayana Buddhism and the development of the image of the Buddha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gandhara sculptures are often made in grey or blue schist stone.

 

• The Buddha in Gandhara art often resembles a Greek god such as Apollo, with wavy hair and robes in folds.

 

• The Gandhara school is also called the Graeco-Buddhist school.

 

• Gandhara covers the area around Peshawar and Rawalpindi, with Taxila as a famous city.

 

• The Gandhara style later spread to Central Asia and influenced Buddhist art in China.

 

NOTE

 

• Chinese elements (Option 1): Chinese elements played no major role in the formation of Gandhara art, even though contacts with China existed through the Silk Route. The mix came from Greek and Roman sources.

 

• Egyptian elements (Option 3): Egyptian elements were not the main outside influence on Gandhara art, which grew out of Greek and Roman artistic styles that came through Bactria and the Roman trade.

 

• Arab elements (Option 4): Arab elements came to India much later, with Islam in the medieval period. They could not have influenced Gandhara art of the first centuries AD.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Gandhara school of art:

1. It began under the Indo-Greek rulers.

2. Its real patrons were the Sakas and Kushanas.

3. Kanishka in particular gave it royal patronage.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Gandhara art began under the Indo-Greeks, its real patrons were the Sakas and Kushanas, and Kanishka gave it royal patronage (गांधार कला — इंडो-ग्रीक से शुरू, कनिष्क का संरक्षण)

 

• The school grew in Peshawar and north-western India, including Taxila.

 

• It blended Indian with Greco-Roman elements and had Mahayana Buddhism as its main theme.

 

• The human body is modelled realistically, with muscles, moustache and curly hair.

 

• Rich carving, elaborate ornamentation and symbolic expression are characteristics of the school.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Gandhara school is the first to carve the Buddha in human form in large numbers.

 

• Taxila is also known for its ancient university and archaeological remains.

 

• The school's sculptures include Bodhisattva figures and stucco heads.

 

• Gandhara art flourished from about the first century AD to the fifth century AD in different phases.

 

• Many Gandhara Buddhas are shown with wavy hair, a moustache and heavy folds of cloth, in the Roman style.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): This grouping accepts statements 1 and 2 but rejects statement 3. Statement 3 is also true, since Kanishka especially gave royal patronage to Gandhara art.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): This choice accepts statements 2 and 3 but rejects statement 1. Statement 1 is also true, because the school began under the Indo-Greek rulers.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): This answer accepts statements 1 and 3 but rejects statement 2. Statement 2 is also true since the Sakas and Kushanas were its real patrons.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Mathura school of art:

1. It grew up at Mathura in modern Uttar Pradesh and flourished in the first century AD.

2. Its Buddha images show a spiritual feeling in the face.

3. It produced images only for Indian patrons.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only statements 1 and 2 hold true: the Mathura school flourished at Mathura in the first century AD and its Buddha images show spiritual feeling; statement 3 is wrong as it also made images for non-Indian patrons (मथुरा कला — आध्यात्मिक भाव)

 

• The Mathura school was a local Indian tradition that took in new ideas under the Kushanas.

 

• The school produced images for both Indian and non-Indian patrons, which makes statement 3 false.

 

• The Gandhara school, in comparison, is known for its realistic human body and Greco-Roman influence.

 

• Mathura was the second capital of Kanishka, and this explains the royal support for the school.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mathura sculptures were made in spotted red sandstone from the local Sikri quarries.

 

• Mathura produced Buddhist, Jain and Hindu images.

 

• The Mathura Buddha and Bodhisattva images were exported to other places like Sarnath and Sravasti.

 

• Kushana art thus developed in two main regional centres, Gandhara in the north-west and Mathura in the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

 

• Mathura art also influenced the later Gupta sculpture at Sarnath.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This pairing accepts statements 2 and 3, but statement 3 is false because Mathura produced images for non-Indian patrons too, and it drops the correct statement 1.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This selection accepts statements 1 and 3, but statement 3 is false and statement 2, about spiritual feeling, is true. So this combination is wrong.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Here the option accepts all three statements, but statement 3 is false. The school's output was for both Indian and non-Indian patrons.

question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the Gandhara school of art?
option_1: Realistic modelling of the human body with muscles, moustache and curly hair
option_2: Mixture of Indian and Greco-Roman elements
option_3: Use of spotted red sandstone as the characteristic stone
option_4: Mahayana Buddhism as the central theme
solution_text:
The correct answer is Use of spotted red sandstone as the characteristic stone.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The use of spotted red sandstone as the characteristic stone is a feature of the Mathura school, not the Gandhara school, so it is the answer to the NOT question (मथुरा कला की लाल बलुआ पत्थर — गांधार की विशेषता नहीं)

 

• Gandhara art models the human body realistically, with muscles, moustache and curly hair.

 

• It mixes Indian and Greco-Roman elements and has rich carving and ornamentation.

 

• Its central theme is Mahayana Buddhism and the development of the image of the Buddha.

 

• Its sculptures are found at Taxila, Peshawar and other north-western sites.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gandhara sculptures are usually in grey schist, stucco and clay.

 

• Mathura sculptures use mottled red sandstone.

 

• Gandhara's Buddha shows Greek-style drapery.

 

• Gandhara figures are usually carved in grey schist or stucco, unlike the red sandstone of Mathura.

 

• Gandhara art is sometimes called the Greco-Buddhist art because it grew out of the Greek and Buddhist contact.

 

NOTE

 

• Realistic modelling of the human body with muscles, moustache and curly hair (Option 1): Realistic modelling of the body with muscles, moustache and curly hair is a true feature of Gandhara art. A NOT-type question needs the false feature, so this cannot be the answer.

 

• Mixture of Indian and Greco-Roman elements (Option 2): The mixture of Indian and Greco-Roman elements is the defining trait of Gandhara art, so this statement is true and cannot be the answer to the NOT-type question.

 

• Mahayana Buddhism as the central theme (Option 4): Mahayana Buddhism is the central theme of Gandhara art and the development of Buddha images. As it is a true feature, it is not the answer to the NOT-type question.

question:
Assertion (A): Buddhism split into the Mahayana and Hinayana sects after the Fourth Buddhist Council.

Reason (R): The council, held under Kanishka at Kundalavana in Kashmir, met to settle questions of Buddhist theology and doctrine.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both are true and R explains A: the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka at Kundalavana met to settle doctrinal questions, after which Buddhism divided into Mahayana and Hinayana (चतुर्थ बौद्ध संगीति — महायान-हीनयान विभाजन)

 

• The council was presided over by Vasumitra and held about 72 AD.

 

• Mahayana introduced the worship of Buddha idols, while Hinayana kept the orthodox older tradition.

 

• The disputes over doctrine at the council help explain the division into two sects.

 

• Kanishka's patronage earned him the title of the Second Ashoka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahayana became dominant in Central and East Asia.

 

• Hinayana (Theravada) survives in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.

 

• The Third Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka.

 

• The Buddhist sects sometimes called Hinayana are today called Theravada by their followers, who live mainly in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.

 

• Mahayana literature is mostly in Sanskrit, while the Theravada canon is in Pali.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This option says R is true but not the correct explanation. In fact the doctrinal disputes that the council met to resolve are the context for the split, so R does explain A.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): This option says A is true but R is false. R is also true, since the council met at Kundalavana in Kashmir under Kanishka to settle questions of doctrine.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): This option says A is false but R is true. A is true, since Buddhism did divide into Mahayana and Hinayana after the council.

question:
Consider the following statements about Rudradaman:

1. He bore the title Mahakshatrapa.

2. He fought the Satavahanas.

3. His Junagadh inscription is in Prakrit.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 stand correct: Rudradaman bore the title Mahakshatrapa and fought the Satavahanas; statement 3 is false because the Junagadh inscription is in pure Sanskrit (रुद्रदामन — महाक्षत्रप, जूनागढ़ अभिलेख संस्कृत में)

 

• Rudradaman was a Saka (Western Kshatrapa) ruler of Gujarat, Malwa and Saurashtra.

 

• His Junagadh (Girnar) inscription is the first and longest inscription in Sanskrit and tells of the repair of the Sudarshana Lake.

 

• The Satavahana king he fought was a contemporary from the Deccan.

 

• The inscription is a major source for the history of the Western Kshatrapas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rudradaman's inscription is dated in the Saka year 72, i.e. AD 150.

 

• Sanskrit inscriptions become common later under the Guptas.

 

• The Western Kshatrapas were finally ended by Chandragupta II.

 

• The Junagadh rock also carries an Ashokan edict, an inscription of Rudradaman and a later record of Skandagupta, covering about seven centuries.

 

• Rudradaman is said to have defeated the Satavahana king twice but spared him because of family ties.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): The chosen option includes statement 3, which is false since the inscription is in Sanskrit, and drops statement 1 about the Mahakshatrapa title, which is true.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This alternative accepts statements 1 and 3 but drops statement 2. Statement 2 is true as Rudradaman fought the Satavahanas, while statement 3 is false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This response accepts all three, but statement 3 is false, because the Junagadh inscription was composed in pure Sanskrit, not in Prakrit.

question: Which of the following scholars is NOT associated with the court of the Kushana king Kanishka?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Patanjali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Patanjali is not associated with Kanishka; he was the priest of the Sunga ruler Pushyamitra and author of the Mahabhasya (पतंजलि — शुंग काल, कनिष्क के दरबार से संबंध नहीं)

 

• Nagarjuna, the philosopher of Sunyavada, is counted among the scholars of Kanishka's age.

 

• Charaka, the physician and author of the Charaka Samhita, belongs to the same court.

 

• Ashvaghosha, the author of the Buddhacharita, was a great poet and dramatist of the Kushana age.

 

• Vasumitra also belonged to this group and presided over the Fourth Buddhist Council.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Patanjali's Mahabhasya is a commentary on Panini.

 

• The Sunga age came before the Kushana age by nearly two centuries.

 

• Kanishka's court is often compared to the Navaratnas of later kings.

 

• Patanjali lived during the Sunga age, around the second century BC, while Kanishka lived in the first and second centuries AD.

 

• The Kushana court is also associated with the Buddhist poet and dramatist Ashvaghosha and the philosopher Nagarjuna.

 

NOTE

 

• Nagarjuna (Option 1): Nagarjuna is a scholar linked with Kanishka's court, known as the Einstein of India. Since the question asks who is NOT associated with Kanishka, he cannot be the answer.

 

• Charaka (Option 2): Charaka is listed among the scholars at Kanishka's court as a famous physician. He is therefore associated with Kanishka, and cannot be the answer here.

 

• Ashvaghosha (Option 3): Ashvaghosha was a poet, philosopher and dramatist who wrote the Buddhacharita and is associated with Kanishka's court. He cannot be the odd one out.
